2

Product and Order Filters

Retrieve targeted rows before joining the full order pathway.

Syntax reference — WHERE, BETWEEN, AND/OR, DISTINCT 
-- Numeric comparison
SELECT *
FROM table_name
WHERE numeric_column > 4.00;

-- AND / OR combine logical tests
SELECT *
FROM table_name
WHERE category_column = 'A' OR category_column = 'B'
ORDER BY name_column;

-- Date BETWEEN (inclusive)
SELECT *
FROM table_name
WHERE date_column BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-01-31';

-- DISTINCT values
SELECT DISTINCT category_column
FROM table_name;

Date values are usually written in YYYY-MM-DD format and wrapped in single quotes. BETWEEN includes both the start and end values.

  1. A3.3.2 WHERE

    List all lunch products that cost more than 4.00.

  2. A3.3.2 AND / OR

    Show every customer from house Ash or Oak, ordered alphabetically by name.

  3. A3.3.2 BETWEEN

    Find order headers paid by Account between 2026-03-05 and 2026-03-12.

  4. A3.3.2 DISTINCT

    Return every distinct payment method used in the canteen.

3

Join the Full Order Path

Move from customers to orders to products through the junction table.

Syntax reference — Multi-table JOIN through junction table 
-- A common multi-table join pattern
SELECT a.name_column, b.date_column, c.item_column, j.quantity_column
FROM parent_table    AS b
INNER JOIN owner_table    AS a ON b.owner_id  = a.owner_id
INNER JOIN junction_table AS j ON b.record_id = j.record_id
INNER JOIN item_table     AS c ON j.item_id   = c.item_id;

-- Add a filter after the joins
SELECT c.item_column, b.date_column
FROM parent_table    AS b
INNER JOIN junction_table AS j ON b.record_id = j.record_id
INNER JOIN item_table     AS c ON j.item_id   = c.item_id
WHERE c.category_column = 'Example'
ORDER BY b.date_column;

When a query crosses several tables, write one JOIN at a time and follow the key path carefully. A junction table usually holds the links between a header record and an item record.

  1. A3.3.2 JOIN 2 tables

    Show the customer name and order date for all orders placed by Zara Ahmed or Mina Patel.

  2. A3.3.2 JOIN 4 tables

    Display every order line with OrderID, customer name, product name, and quantity.

  3. A3.3.2 Filter joined data

    Show only drink items sold on or after 2026-03-07.

  4. A3.3.2 JOIN + ORDER BY

    List every product bought by Aisha Rahman, including the order date, ordered from earliest to latest.

4

DDL, DML, and Performance Thinking

Use structure-changing and row-changing commands deliberately.

Syntax reference — CREATE, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE 
-- Create a new table with a foreign key
CREATE TABLE child_table (
    child_id    INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    parent_id   INTEGER,
    note_text   TEXT,
    start_date  DATE,
    FOREIGN KEY (parent_id) REFERENCES parent_table(parent_id)
);

-- Insert a row
INSERT INTO child_table (child_id, parent_id, note_text, start_date)
VALUES (1, 3, 'Example note', '2026-01-15');

-- Update existing data
UPDATE table_name
SET numeric_column = 1.1
WHERE id_column = 3;

-- Delete one row
DELETE FROM child_table
WHERE child_id = 1;

Always think about how many rows your UPDATE or DELETE will affect. Without a WHERE clause, every row in the table is changed.

  1. A3.3.1 CREATE TABLE

    Create a PROMOTION table with PromotionID as the primary key, plus ProductID, PromoText, and StartDate. Add a foreign key back to PRODUCT.

  2. A3.3.3 INSERT

    Insert one promotion for Muffin.

  3. A3.3.3 UPDATE

    Update the price of Still Water from 1.0 to 1.1.

  4. A3.3.3 DELETE

    Delete the promotion you inserted.

  5. A3.3.3 Performance

    Explain why frequent updates to indexed columns can create extra maintenance work for the database engine.

5

Stretch: Reporting and Denormalization

Use these if your class is ready to move toward HL-style reporting.

Syntax reference — GROUP BY and HAVING 
-- Count rows in each group
SELECT group_column, COUNT(*) AS row_count
FROM table_name
GROUP BY group_column;

-- Use more than one aggregate
SELECT group_column,
       COUNT(*) AS row_count,
       AVG(number_column) AS average_value
FROM table_name
GROUP BY group_column;

-- HAVING filters grouped results
SELECT group_column, COUNT(*) AS row_count
FROM table_name
GROUP BY group_column
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3;

GROUP BY creates one result row per group. WHERE filters individual rows before grouping, while HAVING filters the grouped results afterwards.

  1. A3.3.2 GROUP BY

    Count how many order headers used each payment method.

  2. A3.3.2 HAVING

    Extend the previous query so it returns only payment methods used at least three times.

  3. A3.2.7 Denormalization

    Suggest one denormalized reporting table for the canteen and evaluate the tradeoff between easier read queries and extra redundancy.

Model Answers — Canteen Orders

Section 1 — Normalization and Table Design

1
1NF violation avoided Storing multiple product names in one column (e.g. a comma-separated list) breaks First Normal Form, which requires each column to hold a single atomic value. ORDER_ITEM solves this by giving each product on an order its own row.
2
Update anomaly If the product price changes, every order line containing that product would need updating. Missing even one creates inconsistency — the same product showing different prices in different rows.
3
Composite key in ORDER_ITEM The composite key is (OrderID, ProductID). A customer cannot order the same product twice on the same order as two separate line items — the combination must be unique. This keeps quantity modifications in one row rather than duplicate rows.
4
3NF design Each table stores facts about one entity only. Customer details are in CUSTOMER; order metadata in ORDER_HEADER; product details in PRODUCT. ORDER_ITEM only stores the relationship plus quantity — no repeated customer names or product prices. This removes transitive dependencies.

Section 2 — Product and Order Filters

1 
SELECT * FROM PRODUCT
WHERE Category = 'Lunch' AND Price > 4.00;
2 
SELECT * FROM CUSTOMER
WHERE House = 'Ash' OR House = 'Oak'
ORDER BY CustomerName;
3 
SELECT * FROM ORDER_HEADER
WHERE PaymentMethod = 'Account'
  AND OrderDate BETWEEN '2026-03-05' AND '2026-03-12';
4 
SELECT DISTINCT PaymentMethod FROM ORDER_HEADER;

Section 3 — Join the Full Order Path

1 
SELECT c.CustomerName, oh.OrderDate
FROM ORDER_HEADER oh
INNER JOIN CUSTOMER c ON oh.CustomerID = c.CustomerID
WHERE c.CustomerName IN ('Zara Ahmed', 'Mina Patel');
2 
SELECT oh.OrderID, c.CustomerName, p.ProductName, oi.Quantity
FROM ORDER_HEADER oh
INNER JOIN CUSTOMER   c  ON oh.CustomerID = c.CustomerID
INNER JOIN ORDER_ITEM oi ON oh.OrderID    = oi.OrderID
INNER JOIN PRODUCT    p  ON oi.ProductID  = p.ProductID;
3 
SELECT p.ProductName, oh.OrderDate
FROM ORDER_HEADER oh
INNER JOIN ORDER_ITEM oi ON oh.OrderID   = oi.OrderID
INNER JOIN PRODUCT    p  ON oi.ProductID = p.ProductID
WHERE p.Category = 'Drink'
  AND oh.OrderDate >= '2026-03-07';
4 
SELECT p.ProductName, oh.OrderDate
FROM ORDER_HEADER oh
INNER JOIN CUSTOMER   c  ON oh.CustomerID = c.CustomerID
INNER JOIN ORDER_ITEM oi ON oh.OrderID    = oi.OrderID
INNER JOIN PRODUCT    p  ON oi.ProductID  = p.ProductID
WHERE c.CustomerName = 'Aisha Rahman'
ORDER BY oh.OrderDate ASC;

Section 4 — DDL, DML, and Performance Thinking

1 
CREATE TABLE PROMOTION (
    PromotionID INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    ProductID   INTEGER,
    PromoText   TEXT,
    StartDate   DATE,
    FOREIGN KEY (ProductID) REFERENCES PRODUCT(ProductID)
);
2 
-- Muffin ProductID — check with SELECT first, assume 4
INSERT INTO PROMOTION (PromotionID, ProductID, PromoText, StartDate)
VALUES (1, 4, 'Muffin deal — 2 for 1!', '2026-03-13');
3 
UPDATE PRODUCT SET Price = 1.1 WHERE ProductName = 'Still Water';
4 
DELETE FROM PROMOTION WHERE PromotionID = 1;
5
Index maintenance overhead An index stores a sorted copy of a column to speed up lookups. Every time a row in that column is updated, the index must also be updated to stay in order. Frequent price changes on an indexed Price column would cause constant index rebuilds, using CPU and storage I/O.

Section 5 — Stretch: Reporting and Denormalization

1 
SELECT PaymentMethod, COUNT(*) AS OrderCount
FROM ORDER_HEADER
GROUP BY PaymentMethod;
2 
SELECT PaymentMethod, COUNT(*) AS OrderCount
FROM ORDER_HEADER
GROUP BY PaymentMethod
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3;
3
Denormalized reporting table A CANTEEN_REPORT table could store: OrderDate, CustomerName, House, ProductName, Category, Price, Quantity. Benefit: a daily sales dashboard needs only one SELECT *. Tradeoff: if a product price changes, all historical rows still show the old price unless also updated — creating redundancy and potential inconsistency.
